profile.reading: This facility, CH1, is one of two Element Critical buildings this registry maps to 711 North Edgewood Avenue, Wood Dale, Illinois 60191, in the Chicago metro; the operator maintains separate, dedicated marketing pages for "Chicago One" and "Chicago Two," indicating these are genuinely distinct facilities the company markets separately despite sharing one mapped street address, consistent with a multi-building business park or campus rather than a single structure recorded twice. The operator's own materials associate this record with 151,000 square feet of space and 7 MW of IT capacity, alongside PCI DSS and HIPAA compliance. Element Critical is a privately held colocation operator, rebranded from Central Colo in 2017, backed by an investor group including Mercuria, 26North, Arctos, and Safanad per Mercuria's own press materials, and describes itself as a data center infrastructure provider specializing in high-density power and advanced cooling for demanding workloads including AI and GPU infrastructure, offering colocation from individual cabinets to custom suites supporting deployments up to 50 megawatts across its current three-market portfolio (Austin, Houston, and Chicago). No founding date, year-opened figure, or further building-specific breakdown distinguishing CH1 from CH2 beyond the operator's own separate marketing pages was located in sourcing reachable this session. Wood Dale sits in DuPage County, part of the broader Chicago-area O'Hare-adjacent data center corridor that has drawn colocation and enterprise demand for its proximity to the airport, fiber density, and access to ComEd power infrastructure, alongside other operators tracked elsewhere in this registry. No independent trade-press coverage distinguishing CH1 from CH2 in construction date or expansion history was located this session.

reading.body:
Element Critical CH1 publishes 7 MW of IT capacity across 151,000 square feet in Wood Dale, Illinois, ranking fifth among the six Illinois facilities that disclose power figures and contributing less than 3 percent of the state's published 236 MW total.

The facility's large footprint relative to its power output suggests it was built for lower-density, mixed workloads rather than modern GPU clusters, which demand 40 kW per rack or higher. At that density, 7 MW supports roughly 175 racks, but the square footage implies the campus was not originally optimized for such concentration. This distinction matters because AI training is remaking data center economics, and facilities built for traditional enterprise computing often lack the electrical infrastructure, cooling design, and spatial efficiency that high-density GPU deployments require.

PCI DSS and HIPAA certifications confirm the campus targets regulated workloads in payments and healthcare. Neither certification tracks AI capability. The certifications tell you the operator prioritizes compliance-driven tenants, not that the facility does or does not support AI training or inference.

The data does not disclose whether CH1 currently hosts AI workloads, its utilization rate, or future expansion plans. It does not explain why Illinois, despite its location relative to major tech hubs and power infrastructure, publishes so little disclosed capacity compared to other states. Whether this reflects actual scarcity of AI-capable facilities or merely incomplete public disclosure remains unknown.
